blocks.text: Every day an adult loses billions of cells, among them the cells between developing fingers and the neutrophils that finished fighting an infection, without a trace of inflammation. In contrast, a lung biopsy from a patient with tuberculosis shows a crumbly white centre where tissue has been destroyed and provoked intense inflammation. Both are cell death, but they are different processes with different causes and consequences.

blocks.markdown: Cells die in two broad ways. **Necrosis** is accidental, unregulated death caused by severe injury such as ischaemia, toxins or infection. **Apoptosis** is regulated, energy-dependent 'programmed' cell death that removes cells in development, physiological turnover and certain pathology. The key distinction is that necrosis releases cell contents and triggers inflammation, whereas apoptosis packages the cell for quiet removal.

blocks.title: Necrosis and apoptosis
blocks.text: Necrosis: death of cells in a living tissue after irreversible injury, with membrane rupture, leakage of contents and an inflammatory reaction. Apoptosis: a regulated, ATP-requiring suicide programme executed by caspases, in which the cell shrinks and fragments into apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed without inflammation.

rows: Fragmentation into discrete pieces; chromatin condensation
blocks.caption: Necrosis compared with apoptosis.

blocks.markdown:
### Nuclear changes in necrosis

The nucleus shows one of three changes: **pyknosis** (shrinkage and increased basophilia), **karyorrhexis** (fragmentation) and **karyolysis** (fading of basophilia as DNase digests chromatin). The cytoplasm becomes more eosinophilic because of loss of RNA and denatured protein.

### Patterns of necrosis

**Coagulative necrosis** is typical of ischaemic death in solid organs (heart, kidney, spleen) except the brain. Protein denaturation exceeds enzymatic digestion, so the tissue architecture is preserved as a firm, pale 'ghost' outline for some days. **Liquefactive necrosis** occurs in bacterial abscesses and in the brain after infarction: hydrolytic enzymes digest the dead tissue into a liquid. **Caseous necrosis** is characteristic of tuberculosis and some fungal infections: tissue is a friable, cheese-like white mass that has lost all architecture and is surrounded by a granulomatous inflammatory border. **Fat necrosis** occurs in acute pancreatitis and breast trauma: lipases release fatty acids that combine with calcium to form chalky white **saponification** deposits. **Fibrinoid necrosis** (immune complexes deposited in vessel walls) and **gangrenous necrosis** (coagulative necrosis of a limb with superimposed infection) are also named patterns.

rows: White, cheesy, structureless centre in a granuloma
blocks.caption: Patterns of necrosis by typical setting.

blocks.title: Matching a section to a pattern
blocks.prompt: A pathologist examines a 3 cm pale, wedge-shaped area in a kidney removed after renal artery occlusion. Under the microscope the tubular outlines are visible but the nuclei are absent and the cytoplasm is pink. What pattern is this and why?

steps.text: Identify the tissue and cause: a solid organ other than brain, with ischaemic injury from vascular occlusion.
Look at architecture: tubular outlines are preserved, which means protein denaturation has outpaced enzymatic digestion.
Nuclei absent and eosinophilic cytoplasm are in keeping with necrosis (karyolysis, loss of RNA).

blocks.answer: Coagulative necrosis of ischaemic renal tissue.

blocks.markdown:
### Mechanisms of apoptosis

Apoptosis is executed by **caspases**, proteases that cleave proteins and activate DNases. There are two initiating pathways that converge on the executioner caspases (caspase-3 and caspase-6/7).

The **intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway** is triggered by DNA damage, withdrawal of growth factors or misfolded proteins. Pro-apoptotic proteins (BAX, BAK) permeabilise the mitochondrial membrane, releasing **cytochrome c** into the cytosol. Cytochrome c binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates **caspase-9**. Anti-apoptotic **BCL-2** prevents this; its overexpression (as in follicular lymphoma with t(14;18)) prolongs cell survival.

The **extrinsic (death receptor) pathway** begins when a ligand binds a death receptor on the cell surface, for example **Fas ligand** binding **Fas (CD95)**, or TNF binding TNF receptor 1. Adaptor proteins recruit and activate **caspase-8** (initiator). Cytotoxic T cells also kill by inducing apoptosis: perforin and granzymes enter the target cell and activate caspases directly.

blocks.title: Which pathway?
blocks.prompt: Ionising radiation causes DNA double-strand breaks in the epithelium of a patient's intestinal crypts and many cells die by apoptosis. Identify the pathway, the initiator caspase, and the role of TP53.

steps.text: DNA damage is an internal stress, so the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway is engaged.
The damage-sensing protein TP53 is stabilised and increases transcription of pro-apoptotic BAX and PUMA.
BAX permeabilises mitochondria; cytochrome c is released and forms the apoptosome with Apaf-1.
The apoptosome activates the initiator caspase-9, which activates caspase-3.

blocks.answer: Intrinsic pathway; caspase-9 is the initiator, and TP53 drives pro-apoptotic gene expression.

items: Physiological apoptosis: embryonic digit separation, involution of the lactating breast, turnover of gut epithelium.
Pathological apoptosis: DNA damage, viral hepatitis (Councilman bodies), graft rejection, cytotoxic T-cell killing.
Apoptotic cells are tagged by phosphatidylserine on the outer membrane leaflet so macrophages engulf them.
Too little apoptosis can favour cancer; too much is seen in neurodegeneration and AIDS.

blocks.title: Brain and abscess
blocks.text: Remember that ischaemic death normally gives coagulative necrosis, but the brain is the exception and shows liquefactive necrosis; bacterial abscesses are also liquefactive because neutrophil enzymes digest the tissue.

points: Necrosis is accidental, swells the cell, ruptures the membrane and causes inflammation; apoptosis is regulated, shrinks the cell and does not cause inflammation.
Coagulative, liquefactive, caseous and fat necrosis are linked to ischaemic solid organs, abscess and brain, tuberculosis and pancreatitis respectively.
The intrinsic pathway uses cytochrome c and caspase-9; the extrinsic pathway uses death receptors such as Fas and caspase-8.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?

options.text: The plasma membrane stays intact and cell contents are packaged without inflammation
The cell enlarges before it ruptures
It always affects large contiguous groups of cells
It occurs only after irreversible ischaemia

questions.correctOptionText: The plasma membrane stays intact and cell contents are packaged without inflammation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: apoptotic bodies are phagocytosed without inflammation.
distractorRationale.b: Swelling is a feature of necrosis, while apoptotic cells shrink.
distractorRationale.d: Ischaemia causes necrosis; apoptosis is programmed and regulated.

questions.explanation: Apoptosis is a controlled process in which the membrane remains intact and fragments are tidily removed, so there is no inflammatory response. Cell swelling, group involvement and ischaemic causation describe necrosis.

questions.stem: A section of lung from a patient with tuberculosis shows a granuloma with a central soft, white, amorphous area without any preserved architecture. This is:

distractorRationale.a: Correct: caseous necrosis is the hallmark of tuberculous granulomas.
distractorRationale.c: Fat necrosis is seen in pancreatitis and breast trauma.
distractorRationale.d: Fibrinoid necrosis affects vessel walls in immune-mediated vasculitis.

questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis produces a cheese-like, structureless mass surrounded by granulomatous inflammation and is typical of tuberculosis. Coagulative necrosis would retain tissue outlines.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis develops chalky white spots on the omentum. Release of pancreatic lipase explains this because:

options.text: Fatty acids released from triglycerides combine with calcium (saponification)
Immune complexes deposit in omental arterioles

questions.correctOptionText: Fatty acids released from triglycerides combine with calcium (saponification)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lipases split fat, and the fatty acids form calcium soaps.
distractorRationale.d: Ischaemic protein denaturation gives coagulative necrosis.

questions.explanation: Pancreatic lipases digest triglycerides in fat to glycerol and fatty acids. The fatty acids bind calcium to form insoluble soaps, visible as chalky white areas of fat necrosis.

questions.stem: Which protein released from mitochondria is the key trigger for apoptosome formation in the intrinsic pathway?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cytochrome c binds Apaf-1 to activate caspase-9.
distractorRationale.c: Fas ligand is the extrinsic pathway trigger on the cell surface.
distractorRationale.d: Caspase-8 is the extrinsic pathway initiator.

questions.explanation: Cytochrome c released through BAX/BAK pores binds Apaf-1 and forms the apoptosome that activates caspase-9. BCL-2 does the opposite, blocking this release.

questions.stem: True or false: Overexpression of BCL-2, as in follicular lymphoma, promotes cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis.
questions.explanation: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that stabilises the mitochondrial membrane. Its overexpression after the t(14;18) translocation allows B cells to avoid death and accumulate.

questions.stem: A cytotoxic T cell kills a virus-infected hepatocyte. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Granzymes delivered through perforin pores activate caspases, causing apoptosis
The cell swells and bursts, causing coagulative necrosis
Only the intrinsic pathway can be involved
BCL-2 is required to execute the death

questions.correctOptionText: Granzymes delivered through perforin pores activate caspases, causing apoptosis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: T-cell killing causes apoptosis via granzymes and also death-receptor signalling.
distractorRationale.b: Cytotoxic T-cell killing is apoptotic, not necrotic.
distractorRationale.c: Fas ligand also engages the extrinsic pathway.

questions.explanation: Perforin forms pores through which granzymes enter and activate caspases directly. Cytotoxic T cells can also express Fas ligand, so the extrinsic pathway is also used.

questions.stem: In a liver biopsy examined for viral hepatitis, a pathologist counts 400 hepatocytes in a high-power field. Eight of them are apoptotic (Councilman bodies). Calculate the apoptotic index as a percentage of hepatocytes.
questions.explanation: The apoptotic index is the proportion of cells that are apoptotic: 8/400 = 0.02, or 2%. Counting apoptotic cells relative to the total is a standard way to quantify cell death in tissue.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man dies a week after a large middle cerebral artery infarct. The infarcted area at autopsy is a soft, cavitating area. Which pattern of necrosis explains this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: brain infarcts liquefy because of enzymatic digestion.
distractorRationale.b: This is typical of other solid organs, not brain.
distractorRationale.d: Fat necrosis needs lipases acting on fat.

questions.explanation: The brain has little structural connective tissue and abundant lysosomal enzymes, so ischaemic brain tissue liquefies and leaves a cyst. Other solid organs show coagulative necrosis.

questions.stem: Compare necrosis and apoptosis in terms of cause, cell size, membrane, nuclear change and inflammation.
markingGuide: Necrosis caused by severe injury (ischaemia, toxins); apoptosis by programmed or regulated signals (development, DNA damage, immune killing)
Necrosis: cell swelling; apoptosis: cell shrinkage
Necrosis: membrane disrupted and contents leak; apoptosis: membrane intact, apoptotic bodies
Necrosis: pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis; apoptosis: chromatin condensation and nuclear fragmentation
Necrosis provokes inflammation; apoptosis does not
Apoptosis requires ATP and caspases; necrosis is passive
questions.explanation: A good answer contrasts accidental, inflammatory death with regulated, caspase-driven death. The table of features gives the points.

questions.stem: A tissue contains 2.5 x 10^6 cells. Apoptosis removes 1.2% of cells per day and mitosis adds cells so that the total remains constant. How many cells per day must mitosis add? Give the answer in cells per day, in units of 10^3 cells/day.
questions.explanation: To hold the population constant, cell gain must equal cell loss: 1.2% of 2.5 x 10^6 = 30,000 cells per day, which is 30 in units of 10^3. This is the principle of tissue homeostasis, in which regulated apoptosis balances proliferation.
